articles.title_orig: Passenger flights diverted as Kuwait intercepts Iranian drone attack
articles.title_zh: Passenger flights diverted as Kuwait intercepts Iranian drone attack
articles.content_orig:
Flights on the key air traffic corridor between Europe, the Gulf region and Asia crossing Iraq towards the Gulf were suddenly redirected south on Thursday afternoon amid reports that Kuwait’s airspace was closed.
The Kuwait military has since issued a statement that four people were injured after "a number of hostile" Iranian drones were detected and intercepted in its airspace.
"The Iranian aggression targeted a vital facility, causing falling shrapnel that injured four people," said a statement by the defence ministry, adding that the injured were taken to a hospital for treatment while the incident caused unspecified "material damage".
Two Italians working for German defence group Rheinmetall died, Italy's foreign ministry said.
Since the war in Iran broke out in late February, most international flights crossing Europe have been flying toward major hubs in Doha, Abu Dhabi, Dubai and other destinations via a route running through Turkey, Iraq, Kuwait, Bahrain and the UAE.
All flights on the corridor were given a new heading, prompting them to make a sharp turn ahead of Kuwait's airspace and move the entire international corridor toward neighbouring countries, including a flight on which Euronews reporters were travelling.
The drone attack on Kuwait comes just one day after the US Virtual Embassy in Iran said Tehran, Yemen's Houthis and other aligned groups may target US interests and citizens in the region, including companies and institutions.
Washington warned citizens across the Middle East to exercise heightened vigilance after Iran attacked US assets in Bahrain and Kuwait and Yemen's Houthi forces struck a tower in Riyadh's financial district, wounding 11 people.
US citizens in the region were urged to monitor airline and airport operations and prepare for possible flight cancellations and airspace closures.
The war has seen the Gulf states caught in the crossfire, with US military facilities and energy installations on their soil targeted.
The US and Iran are in a standoff over the vital Strait of Hormuz, with the US military working to escort ships transiting the waterway in defiance of Tehran's attempts to close it.
Flights bound for the Gulf countries carry extra fuel for emergency diversions, in case they need to enter a holding pattern near their destinations if airports and airspaces close due to military activity.

articles.title_orig: Spain’s far right hasn’t governed since Franco. Immigration fears could change that
articles.title_zh: Spain’s far right hasn’t governed since Franco. Immigration fears could change that
articles.content_orig:
Andalusia, Spain – Surrounded by shelves heaving with canned goods and cured meats, the owners of a family-run grocery store are locked in a debate about Spain’s upcoming elections.
All politicians are “liars”, proclaims 32-year-old Antonio Cerezo, announcing he will cast a blank ballot. His cousin, Patricia Nicolas Cerezo, 43, is less certain, riddled with doubt about who to support.
As for her 18-year-old son, first-time voter Alfonso Duque, the only choice is the far-right Vox party : “It can’t get worse than this”.
The one thing that the family in the small village of Rioja seems to agree on is that Prime Minister Pedro Sanchez’s socialists must go.
A former socialist bastion, the southern region’s political landscape has changed. Since May’s regional election, it has been governed by a coalition of the conservative People’s Party (PP) and Vox, once a fringe party that has drawn support by championing migrant deportations and tapping into a wider wave of far-right, anti-establishment support across Europe.
Ahead of Sunday’s snap vote, observers say Andalusia’s political dynamics could offer a glimpse of what might come next nationally.
That arrangement could soon be tested at the national level.
Opinion polls put the PP first, followed by Sanchez’s Socialists (PSOE), with Vox third.
The PP is projected to fall short of an outright majority, but together the two right-wing parties are expected to have enough seats to govern.
PP leader Alberto Nunez Feijoo has indicated that he would prefer to lead a minority government with Vox’s backing in parliament, while leaving open the possibility of a coalition like the one in Andalusia.
Tucked away between rows of greenhouses and arid mountains in the southern region of Andalusia, Rioja is home to about 1,600 people.
Overlooking the plains framing the quaint village is a giant silhouette of a bull. For much of Francisco Franco’s dictatorship , this area remained poor and largely agricultural.
As machines took over more of the work in the fields, many Andalusians left for jobs in industrial centres such as Barcelona and Madrid. In the mid-seventies, the Socialists found fertile ground in a society that had long felt marginalised and neglected.
In 1982, the PSOE won an absolute majority in Andalusia’s first regional election, beginning a stretch in power that lasted more than three decades.
But by 2018, the Socialists’ hold on the southern region was starting to crack.
A series of corruption scandals tarnished the party’s image, benefitting the PP. The PSOE still came first in that year’s regional election, but the conservatives took power with the backing of the liberal Ciudadanos and Vox.
“For the first time, the PP opened the door to the far-right to be able to govern – that created a precedent for everything that happens today nationwide,” said Bosco Govantes, political science associate professor at Sevilla’s Universidad Pablo de Olavide. “Before, there was a red line, a stigma, over collaborating with the far right. But that move in Andalusia kicked off the normalisation of Vox’s narrative.”
The party was founded in 2013 when a group of ultraconservatives, led by Santiago Abascal, broke up with the conservatives they accused of being too indulgent towards Catalan separatists.
Vox at first struggled to get into the political mainstream, but entered Andalusia’s regional parliament in 2018.
Once the Catalan issue faded from the national debate, the party shifted its focus to migration.
Abascal accuses Sanchez of enabling what he calls “a migrant invasion” to “replace the Spanish people” as the Socialist government adopted an open-door policy and legalised undocumented migrants who had worked in Spain for years.
Since the start of Sanchez’s rule to last year, the number of foreign-born residents in Spain rose from 6.3 million to 10.4 million, official figures show. He takes pride in the policy, as Spain’s GDP grew under his tenure.
Vox, the likely kingmaker that is expected to increase its vote share more than any other party compared with the 2023 elections, wants to reverse those policies.
Some observers say the conservative party has had to harden its discourse, such as calling for stricter measures against migrants, to stop haemorrhaging voters to its right.
Polling by Ipsos suggested up to 20 percent of Spaniards who voted for the PP in the 2023 elections intended to vote for Vox on Sunday.
Sanchez has pitched the election as a battle between progress and regression, warning that PP and Vox “only agree when it comes to cutting back rights”.
But that argument falls flat in parts of Andalusia, where some do not fear a Vox-PP deal.
“I don’t mind if Vox is in government,” said Rosaria, a 69-year-old retired housewife, while adjusting her white scarf with a red floral pattern. “The PP will keep them in check. It’s a party with vision and structure”.
Sanchez warns that Vox wants to roll back women’s rights.
The issue of gender violence divides the two parties.
Last year, the PP backed the renewal of Spain’s cross-party pact on gender-based violence.
Vox wants to repeal the 2004 gender-based violence law, which protects women from abuse by current or former partners. The party argues that the law discriminates against men and wants to replace it with legislation covering domestic violence regardless of the victim’s sex.
At an event against gender-based violence, Rioja’s PP mayor Olga Maria Gonzalez Jurado was asked how the two parties were getting on in government in Andalusia.
“I think it’s going well,” she said, but she deflected questions on whether the PP had hardened its stance on immigration to keep up with Vox.
In Andalusia, the two parties have been pushing for stricter housing rules for non-Spanish applicants.
Councils can already give people who live or work locally priority for subsidised housing, regardless of nationality. Last month, the two parties backed a non-binding motion urging Madrid to give Spanish citizens priority for subsidised housing and housing aid. Their regional coalition deal also pledges to give people with longstanding ties to Andalusia or Spain priority for public benefits and social housing.
In other regions, the two parties’ cooperation has reached classrooms and places of worship. Aragon dropped a school programme teaching Arabic and Moroccan culture this year and Andalusia is due to follow in 2027.
In the Murcia town of Jumilla, Muslims held Eid al-Fitr prayers in a car park after PP and Vox backed restrictions on the use of municipal sports facilities. The restrictions have drawn criticism over their impact on Muslim religious gatherings.
In Valencia, the parties backed a rule requiring meat served in school canteens to come from animals stunned before slaughter, which still allows halal meals that meet the requirement. In the Balearic Islands, they voted to send Spain’s Congress a bill to ban the burqa [full-face veils sometimes worn by Muslim women that hide the entire face, including eyes] and niqab [similar, but the eyes are visible] in public spaces.
Vox has called for the deportation of foreigners it says, among other grounds, also live on public benefits. This measure – to remove someone with a valid right to stay – has no equivalent in Europe.
The party’s policies have left migrants on edge.
Yudy Ramirez is from Colombia and entered Spain four years ago. For years, took care of her child while juggling two jobs as an in-house caregiver and fruit picker at a greenhouse in Almeria for five euros per hour.
In June, the 49-year-old finally received legal papers.
“Many of us are scared, because returning is not in the plans at the moment,” she said.
Still, not all migrants are targeted in the same way.
Vox’s rhetoric has an ethno-racial undertone which looks at Spanish-speaking foreigners coming from Latin America in more favourable terms as they belong to an Iberosphere which connects far-right movements in the Latin world whose centre is occupied by Vox.

articles.title_orig: Thailand's Bangchak shuts all units at Bangkok refinery after fire, says 9 workers injured
articles.title_zh: Thailand's Bangchak shuts all units at Bangkok refinery after fire, says 9 workers injured
articles.content_orig:
An explosion and fire at a major oil facility in Bangkok injures at least nine people and forces nearby residents to evacuate briefly
BANGKOK -- An explosion and fire at a major oil facility in the Thai capital on Thursday injured at least nine people and forced nearby residents to briefly evacuate, authorities said.
Most of the injured suffered burns and three people were in critical condition, according to Erawan Medical Center in Bangkok. Video posted on social media showed thick black smoke rising from the site in an eastern neighborhood of Bangkok.
A mobile phone alert sent to residents said the incident happened around 3 p.m. and advised people to avoid the area. The city authority reported less than an hour later that the ensuing fire was put out.
Officials later said nearby residents can return home, but advised those living in a 5-kilometer (3-mile) radius of the facility to be cautious of air pollution.
The Pollution Control Department said it sent officials to assess air and water quality in the surrounding area.
Bangchak Corp., which owns the refining and storage facility, confirmed the fire in a Facebook post and said that the cause was still being investigated. The company also said it has halted all production operations.
Energy Minister Akanat Promphan said the fire appeared to start at one of the refinery units, which is about 100 meters (330 feet) away from the oil storage. He said he would inspect the site to ensure there's no further risk.
“If we're not a hundred percent certain that the oil storage is safe, we won't allow them to resume operations,” he said.
Akanat said Thailand's oil supply should not be affected, as there are five other refineries in the country and this facility is not among the biggest.
The refinery, with a listed capacity of 120,000 barrels a day, is the fifth biggest in Thailand and the only one situated in an urban area.
An explosion and fire at the refinery in July 2012 caused damage in a nearby residential neighborhood and it took two weeks to repair the facility.

articles.title_orig: iPhone 20 Pro Could Feature Ceramic in Limited-Edition Model
articles.title_zh: iPhone 20 Pro Could Feature Ceramic in Limited-Edition Model
articles.content_orig:
Apple could offer a limited-edition iPhone 20 Pro model that incorporates ceramic, according to the Chinese leaker known as Fixed Focus Digital.
In a post on Weibo , the leaker claimed to have gotten their hands on ceramic components for the 20th-anniversary iPhone, which is expected to launch next year. The leaker said that production capacity for the components is planned to be very low, suggesting they will be for a limited-edition model.
In a follow-up comment, the leaker claimed that the project would enter mass production if it passes engineering validation testing (EVT), and even joked that its scarcity could make it appreciate in value.
The leaker doesn't say what kind of ceramic components they have in their possession, leaving it unclear whether Apple is considering a ceramic rear panel, a larger section of the enclosure, or a smaller exterior part.
Apple already offers ceramic as a premium casing material on the Apple Watch Series 12, which comes in Pearl White and Night Blue ceramic alongside aluminum and titanium options. The company also previously sold ceramic Apple Watch Edition models, including a white ceramic version of the Series 5.
Interestingly, the ‌iPhone Air‌ features Ceramic Shield 2 on the front and Ceramic Shield on the back, and Fixed Focus Digital has previously said next year's iPhone 20 Pro models will use the same glass design , but with more pronounced curves along all four sides of a titanium frame. Ceramic Shield incorporates tiny ceramic crystals within a glass matrix, which preserves transparency while improving durability. However, the wording of the leaker's latest post suggests that ceramic could be applied in a more visually prominent way.
Apple's 20th-anniversary iPhone models are expected to launch in the fall of 2027 with a radical glass-centric redesign featuring a quad-curved display . Leakers have variously referred to the device as the "iPhone 20 Pro," but Apple's naming plans remain unclear. The company could well skip the iPhone 19 name to emphasize the anniversary, similar to when it introduced the iPhone X in 2017.

The head of the EU Commission, Ursula Von Der Leyen, called for more pressure on Iran Thursday after two Italians were killed in a drone attack in Kuwait.
In a social media post , she said she was "saddened by the news," adding: "We must step up pressure on Iran to put an end to these unacceptable attacks against its neighbours and our partners in the Gulf."
"Today's events are yet another reminder that security in the Gulf is a matter of security for us all," she added.
Italian Foreign Minister Antonio Tajani said earlier that the two technicians were killed in an Iranian attack targeting a Kuwaiti military facility, according to the Italian news agency ANSA.
Speaking in the Italian Senate, Tajani said the drones targeted Kuwaiti military installations at around 2 p.m. local time, including the facility where the two technicians were working.
Italian Foreign Minister Antonio Tajani said on Thursday that two Italian workers were killed in Kuwait in an Iranian attack targeting a Kuwaiti military facility, according to the Italian news agency ANSA.
Speaking in the Italian Senate, Tajani said the drones targeted Kuwaiti military installations at around 2 p.m., including the facility where the two technicians were working.
"There was a powerful explosion and, unfortunately, according to the information reaching us from Kuwait, both of our fellow citizens have died," he said.
Earlier on Thursday, Kuwait's armed forces said several Iranian drones were intercepted, "causing shrapnel to fall and injure four people."
Kuwait's armed forces said several Iranian drones were intercepted Thursday in the small Persian Gulf nation's airspace, "causing shrapnel to fall and injure four people."
"The Iranian aggression targeted a vital site," the Kuwaiti Defense Ministry spokesman Staff Col. Saud Abdulaziz Al-Atwan said in a statement , without offering any further information about what had been targeted.
Al-Atwan identified the four people injured by falling debris as one Kuwaiti national, two Italians and one Pakistani national, and he said "the incident also caused material damage," again without any further detail.
The body of a Jordanian sailor who was reported missing after an Iranian attack on his vessel in the Strait of Hormuz last week was found off the coast of Ras Al Khaimah in the United Arab Emirates, Jordan's Foreign Ministry said on Thursday .
"The body of Mohamed Hossam al-Din al-Otaibi , may he rest in peace, was found on Wednesday," the ministry said.
The United Arab Emirates' state-owned ADNOC energy company reported the sailor missing last week after one of its vessels was attacked in the Strait of Hormuz. It said 11 crew members were injured in the attack.
The Jordanian ministry praised the efforts of UAE and Omani authorities for locating the sailor's body.
Iran's Islamic Revolutionary Guard Corps claimed Thursday that two "non-compliant" oil tankers were on fire after striking sea mines while attempting to transit the Strait of Hormuz via southern shipping lanes the U.S. military insists are safe, but Tehran has repeatedly warned vessels to avoid.
"Since the early hours of today, two non-compliant oil tankers have exploded and caught fire after striking naval mines north of the port of Khasab," which is on the Omani coast in the center of the strait, Iranian state media quoted the IRGC as saying.
The report, which was not immediately corroborated by independent maritime agencies, said one of the ships was a supertanker laden with more than 2 million barrels of crude oil that was left burning after hitting a mine.
The statement — the latest in a series of daily claims by the Iranian regime of ships striking mines in the strait —   came after IRGC Navy commander Rear Adm. Ali Azmaei reiterated Tehran's warning to shipping firms that passage through the strait would only be safe "by respecting Iran's sovereignty."
"We not only have control of this waterway, but have also placed the power to change the equations at the heart of the Strait of Hormuz," declared Azmaei, whose remarks were also carried by state media.
Ship transits through the Strait of Hormuz have fallen again this month and the amount of crude oil and other products shipped outside the Persian Gulf remains at just over half of pre-war levels, according to data from shipping intelligence company Kpler.
The number of ships making the journey per week fell from 217 to 147 between Nov. 1 and Nov. 23, Kpler said in two reports this week.
Tanker crossings averaged 11 per day for the week ending Nov. 21, compared to 50 per day before the war, meanwhile, though the company noted that many crossings are "dark," or done with their AIS transmission systems turned off, usually for safety reasons.
The International Maritime Organization has recorded 141 attacks on commercial ships in and around the strait since the war began in February, including at least 15 in November. October was the worst month for attacks on vessels in the region since the war began, with at least 35 ships coming under attack according to the IMO.
The U.K. navy's Maritime Trade Operations agency said late Wednesday that it had received a report of an explosion near a tanker about 50 nautical miles west of Dubai, in the United Arab Emirates, west of the entrance to the Strait of Hormuz.
The tanker's master reported an explosion, which UKMTO attributed to an "unknown projectile," but the vessel was not damaged and there was no environmental impact, UKMTO said in an advisory .
Iran claimed earlier Wednesday, without offering evidence or details, that a liquefied natural gas carrier had struck a sea mine in the southern part of the strait — the latest in a series of similar daily claims.
Iran insists all vessels must use northern shipping lanes through the strait, and only with authorization from its military. The regime said Wednesday that it was tightening its control over the vital waterway, which the U.S. military insists is safe and open to traffic.
Yemen's Houthis said Wednesday they had targeted the Saudi ports of Jeddah and Jazan in response to Saudi strikes on a Yemeni port controlled by the Iran-backed group as their conflict further escalated.
The attacks came after the Saudi-led military coalition fighting the Houthis said it had struck Yemen's Red Sea port city of Hodeida, drawing threats of retaliation from the Yemeni fighters.
"Both operations resulted in damage to the targeted sites," Houthi military spokesman Yahya Saree said.
An explosion was later heard in Saudi capital Riyadh, according to an AFP journalist and residents, after authorities issued an alert warning of a "hostile aerial threat," which was lifted shortly after.
Residents in northern and eastern Riyadh confirmed hearing the blast, with one saying their house windows "shook violently."
Saudi forces said air defenses destroyed two ballistic missiles launched toward the capital by the Houthis, as well as a cruise missile in the western part of the country and a drone near Jeddah's port.
Turki al-Malki, the spokesman for the Saudi-led military coalition battling the Houthis, said no civilian injuries resulted from the debris of the intercepted drone.
In recent weeks, the Houthis have launched a barrage at Saudi targets including the financial district, airports, energy infrastructure and military sites.
The Saudi coalition has in turn been striking Houthi-held areas of Yemen in support of the internationally recognized government, which has been battling the Houthis for territory since a civil war reignited in July.

articles.title_orig: Global stocks rise and tech shares rebound as US closes for Thanksgiving
articles.title_zh: Global stocks rise and tech shares rebound as US closes for Thanksgiving
articles.content_orig:
Global stocks rallied on Thursday, staging a tentative recovery from an intense AI-driven sell-off and looked past a fresh set of tariffs unveiled by the White House on Wednesday.
U.S. markets will be closed Thursday for the Thanksgiving holiday and will have a shortened trading session on Friday. During Wednesday's regular session, the Dow gained 0.33%, the tech-heavy Nasdaq Composite fell 0.62% and the S&P 500 shed 0.25%, with the major averages paring losses seen earlier in the trading day.
In Europe on Thursday, equities rose sharply. The pan-European Stoxx 600 was 1.6% higher by 12:20 p.m. in London (7:20 a.m. ET), with all sectors and major bourses in positive territory.
Germany's DAX led gains on a rise of 1.9%, while the Stoxx 600 Technology index jumped 2.5%. The regional tech index has lost around 12% so far this month, amid jitters around a potential AI bubble bursting and the ousting — and return — of Jensen Huang as Nvidia CEO.
German semiconductor firm Infineon was more than 4% higher in afternoon trading, as chip stocks notched a boost. ASMI and ASML each gained just over 3%, while Be Semiconductor added 3.5%.
Asia-Pacific markets also rose on Thursday, with regional tech stocks also rebounded sharply, led by Japanese chip-related companies.
South Korea's Kospi gained 0.29% to close at 4,711.21, while the small-cap Kosdaq index advanced 0.78% to 655.71 after the country's central bank hiked benchmark lending rates to a 2-year high in its final meeting of the year.
Japan's Nikkei 225 rose 0.86% to 57,499.16 while the Topix edged 0.11% higher to 3,750.4. Australia's S&P/ASX 200 gained 0.82% to 8,763.8.
Hong Kong's Hang Seng index was up 1.52% in its last hour of trade, while mainland China's CSI 300 edged higher marginally, closing at 3,900.55.
SoftBank Group surged more than 7%, while chip-testing equipment maker Advantest rose 4.57%. Lasertec and Disco gained , while Tokyo Electron climbed 0.59%
In South Korea, memory chip giants SK Hynix and Samsung Electronics advanced more than 2% and 0.35%, respectively. The gains followed a bruising session Wednesday amid renewed concerns over the sustainability of artificial intelligence spending.
Russ Mould, investment director at AJ Bell, labeled it a "solid day" for regional markets, suggesting investors were hunting for opportunities in the wake of an intense global sell-off.
"The rollercoaster stock market is back on an upwards path as a new round of Trump tariffs aren't as bad as feared and the US takes the day off to celebrate Thanksgiving," he said in a note on Thursday morning. "It was notable that investors cast their net wide for opportunities, fishing for bargains in the rubble following the tech sell-off and looking at other sectors in the quest for diversification."
But Mould warned investors not to be "too complacent."
"Oil prices heading higher is not good for efforts to tame inflation, neither is the prospect of retaliation by countries on the receiving end of new US tariffs," he said.
The Trump administration on Wednesday unveiled a fresh barrage of tariffs on more than a dozen trading partners, including China, the European Union and India.
Daniela Hathorn, senior financial market analyst at Capital.com, said in a Thursday note that the mood in markets was "cautious rather than uniformly negative."
"European markets are attempting to rebound after yesterday's decline, while U.S. cash markets are closed for Thanksgiving, limiting the chance to test whether Wall Street's late recovery can hold," she said. "The main focus now will be trying to determine how many further increases the Fed considers necessary in early 2027 and whether AI shares can withstand that rate path while investors continue to question the returns on heavy spending."
U.S. inflation data on Wednesday reinforced expectations of further monetary tightening by the Federal Reserve. The personal consumption expenditures price index rose 3.8% year on year in October, accelerating from 3.7% in September, while core inflation came in slightly above expectations at 3.3%.
Mark Haefele, chief investment officer at UBS Global Wealth Management, said in a note on Thursday morning that his team believes investors should maintain strategic allocations to equities.
But he advised market participants to "review current allocations and use market moves as an opportunity to rebalance, refocus, and strengthen portfolio resilience."

articles.title_orig: Government's antisemitism adviser launches investigation into BBC
articles.title_zh: Government's antisemitism adviser launches investigation into BBC
articles.content_orig:
The government's antisemitism adviser has launched an investigation into the BBC over allegations of a "hostile work environment" for Jews.
Lord Mann told BBC Radio 4's Today programme he had decided to open the investigation "because there seems to be a growing feeling of discomfort among Jewish staff".
He said: "If that's true, and that's what I'm going to attempt to find out, and if that is widespread, then that's a really serious problem that has to be addressed. And I don't hear and see that being addressed, and at a senior level."
The BBC said it takes "any and all allegations of discrimination extremely seriously – there is no place for it at the BBC".
The corporation said it had introduced compulsory antisemitism training for all staff, and said "we actively encourage colleagues to report any incidences or concerns they have".
The BBC statement added that it is "determined to ensure the BBC is a place where everyone can be themselves and feel accepted".
The Department for Culture, Media and Sport told the BBC: "This government will not tolerate antisemitism. It has no place in our society.
"The BBC has a crucial role in ensuring all communities are heard and feel valued as part of our public life. That is the standard that we expect the BBC to be held to. We will consider Lord Mann's independent report carefully when we receive it."
Lord Mann, who was appointed by former Prime Minister Theresa May as an independent adviser on antisemitism in 2019 , said anyone contacting him would have "total anonymity guaranteed".
"I have no agenda against the BBC," he told Today, calling himself "an entirely blank sheet of paper".
"Some of the things that I'm being told have been quite disturbing sometimes, how little the senior manager of the BBC seem to get it, and so I'm opening this up," he said.
"Look, there is a problem. The question is - is the problem just a few people? Is it a problem that's easily solved? But if it's an institutional problem, that's much deeper and more difficult to solve. It may be. I'll report the facts."
The former MP said he had previously "made suggestions" to the corporation after he had "repeatedly met" Jewish staff.
He said the things "the BBC has done to try and sort things out have not worked".
His agenda was "ensuring the BBC meets its charter obligations", saying "people are fearful... of expressing their concerns internally, that's the problem".
Lord Mann's remit as the government's independent adviser on antisemitism includes "to engage proactively with the Jewish community and institutions".
He said he plans to have his investigation "totally completed and reported to the BBC and the government before Easter".
He previously conducted a review into antisemitism and racism in the NHS , which was commissioned by the health secretary and which reported in June.
The Guardian recently reported that BBC deputy director general Rhodri Talfan Davies said he did not accept that an independent inquiry into antisemitism was needed.
"We have very, very robust processes – we review them regularly," he told members of the Broadcasting Press Guild earlier this month.
"Of course in any large organisation there can be instances of discrimination, which you deal with when they arise, but there is no evidence of any systemic issue within the BBC that would merit anything like that.
"I don't believe there is institutional discrimination of any sort in the BBC, but I think as an organisation you always have to look harder and review how you go about identifying issues, and that work is never done."
The Board of Deputies of British Jews said in a statement that it welcomed the review into "deeply concerning" experiences of Jewish staff at the BBC.
"The BBC is an important national institution and should be setting the gold standard for an inclusive workplace and impartial broadcasting," it said.
"We stand ready to support both Lord Mann and the BBC in addressing these concerns, rebuilding confidence within the Jewish community and ensuring that the BBC sets an example for other broadcasters to follow."
Last month, Oscar-winning producer Lucie Kon said the BBC had given her a £400,000 payout after she raised antisemitism concerns.
The BBC said it did not uphold allegations of antisemitism but accepted there were "shortcomings" in how it treated Kon, which had a "personal impact" on her. The corporation did not specify what the shortcomings were.
In January, the BBC apologised for its use of language during coverage of Holocaust Memorial Day, saying programmes should have referred to "six million Jewish people" having been murdered by the Nazi regime, rather than "six million people" or "six million mostly Jewish people".
Last September, the BBC's broadcast of Bob Vylan's controversial set at Glastonbury broke editorial guidelines in relation to harm and offence , with the corporation's complaints unit ruling that some comments could "fairly be characterised as antisemitic". The band denied being antisemitic.

articles.title_orig: Ukraine says it has intercepted a Russian jet-powered drone with a laser for the first time
articles.title_zh: Ukraine says it has intercepted a Russian jet-powered drone with a laser for the first time
articles.content_orig:
Ukraine has used a laser weapon to shoot down a Russian jet-powered attack drone for the first time, a senior military adviser to President Volodymyr Zelenskyy said Wednesday, marking a potentially significant development in the country's effort to defend cities from Russia's daily aerial attacks.
The interception was carried out using the Blysk laser air defense system, which was developed and manufactured by Ukrainian defense technology firm Carmine Sky. Technology for laser air defense systems is being developed as part of the wider Private Air Defense program, Zelenskyy's adviser Serhii "Flash" Beskrestnov   said in a statement .
About 100 companies across Ukraine have joined the government-backed private air defense initiative.
Russia started deploying jet-powered drones in its attacks on Ukraine earlier this year. The weapons travel faster, making them harder to intercept than the more common propeller-driven attack drones.
In June, Ukraine was only intercepting about 57% of the jet-powered drones , reflecting a significant vulnerability as Ukrainian forces had been shooting down about 90% of the conventional Russian attack drones.
Russia has increasingly used its Geran-4 and Geran-5 jet-powered drones in its attacks on Ukraine. Come Back Alive, a Ukrainian military nonprofit group, told CBS News in September that Russia was likely to produce some 1,200 Geran-4 and 800 Geran-5 drones during that month alone, and it projected those numbers would grow each month.
The laser interception reported by Beskrestnov   this week gives some insight into Ukraine's mounting efforts to adapt both its offenses and defenses as Russia's weapons and tactics evolve.
Ukraine has pioneered battlefield drone technology, and it has started building partnerships to export that knowledge and its hardware around the world. In October, Ukrainian forces carried out a world-first aerial drone medical evacuation from the front line.
Ukraine started testing laser air defense systems over the summer. According to Beskrestnov, the Blysk system was used to protect critical infrastructure, though he declined to give more specifics.
He said a number of Ukrainian companies, including Carmine Sky, are working to develop laser technology, but he cautioned that "it is still too early to talk about serial production of the laser."
"Tests are underway, during which lasers protect critical infrastructure facilities," he said.

articles.title_orig: I am staunchly pro-choice – but abortion statistics in the latest sexual attitudes survey shocked even me | Zoe Williams
articles.title_zh: I am staunchly pro-choice – but abortion statistics in the latest sexual attitudes survey shocked even me | Zoe Williams
articles.content_orig:
Young Britons are having half as much sex as they were in 1990, according to a new study, with the average reported frequency falling from four times a month to just twice a month.
The data was produced as part of a long-running study known as the National Survey of Sexual Attitudes and Lifestyles (Natsal), according to a statement Wednesday from the London School of Hygiene & Tropical Medicine (LSHTM), which participates in the research.
“The sex lives of people in Britain have changed markedly since 1990 and they have substantial and varied sexual and reproductive health needs,” LSHTM said.
Researchers randomly selected around 6,700 people from England, Scotland and Wales aged 16-59 to participate in interviews and online surveys between September 2022 and January 2024.
This is the fourth edition of “one of the largest studies of sexual behaviour in the world,” which has previously been undertaken in 1990, 2000 and 2010.
In addition to adults under 45 years old reporting that they are having sex half as much as their peers did in 1990, the survey showed that 77% of 16-59-year-olds reported having sex in the past year, and 89% said they had sex at least once in their lives.
Among 16-24-year-olds, one in three said they had never had sex, up from around one in five in 2010.
Half of young women reported watching pornography in the past 12 months, compared with nearly 90% of male respondents. This was the first time the survey had asked about the use of online pornography.
Attitudes toward children and contraception are also changing. While the use of hormonal contraception declined among young women, the proportion of women who report that they don’t want children has doubled in the past decade.
The survey also reveals important findings for preventing the spread of sexually transmitted infections (STIs), with more than one in four sexually experienced 16-24-year-olds with exclusively opposite-sex partners reporting behaviors that are associated with STI risk.
These include “having four or more partners or condomless sex with two or more partners in the past year or overlapping partners in the past five years,” the statement said.
Men’s sexual health can predict heart issues
“While most adults are having sex, people are having sex less often and more young people have never had sex,” Soazig Clifton, academic director for Natsal at University College London, which also participates in the survey, said in the statement.
“There is also a higher proportion of people reporting same-sex experiences, and online sexual activity is now part of everyday life for many.”
Dr Otilia Mårdh, a scientific officer at the European Centre for Disease Prevention and Control (ECDC), who was not involved in the research, said that “another notable Natsal-4 finding is, that the proportion of men reporting both same-sex and opposite-sex partners (MSWM) more than doubled, from 0.9% (Natsal-3) to 2.3%.”
Feeling like a late bloomer when it comes to sex? There’s hope
“The authors note that this growing population could increasingly bridge sexual networks with different STI risks,” Mårdh said in a comment published by the Science Media Centre on Wednesday.
She added that this is “particularly relevant” as surveillance data from European monitoring programs shows “recent increases in syphilis and gonorrhoea among heterosexual populations, alongside rising congenital syphilis — contrasting with historically lower levels.”
“These trends highlight the need for accessible, stigma-free sexual health services offering prevention and testing tailored to people’s needs,” said Mårdh.
Five papers drawing on the results of the survey were published in the journal The Lancet.

articles.title_orig: Denny's brings back plaque celebrating Nvidia chief Jensen Huang
articles.title_zh: Denny's brings back plaque celebrating Nvidia chief Jensen Huang
articles.content_orig:
Jensen Huang is back at the helm of Nvidia — and Denny's has a booth waiting for him.
The American diner chain welcomed the billionaire's return as Nvidia CEO by revealing that it had reinstated a commemorative plaque marking the birthplace of the artificial intelligence chip giant after learning of its removal on Nov. 13.
"Some things you just don't take off the menu. Jensen Huang is one of them," Denny's said in a post on X .
The plaque marks the booth at a Denny's restaurant in Silicon Valley, California, where Huang and his co-founders discussed the idea for Nvidia, which was founded in 1993.
The restaurant chain said it learned on Nov. 13, a day after Huang's resignation , that the plaque had been removed.
"We put the plaque right back up where it belongs," Denny's said, without specifying who had removed it or why.
Huang's ties to the diner chain, however, stretch back well before Nvidia's founding. He worked at Denny's as a teenager, washing dishes and serving customers before going on to build one of the world's most valuable companies.
The restaurant chain also disclosed that it had contacted Nvidia's communications team on Nov. 10 to express its pride in their shared history.
Huang's return came less than two weeks after his sudden resignation rattled investors and raised questions about corporate governance and succession planning at the chipmaker.
While his return has put those issues in the spotlight, Denny's offered a simpler message to its former employee.
"Jensen, your booth is waiting and the coffee's on. We're always open, 24/7," the restaurant chain said.

articles.title_orig: US warns EU leaders against Big Tech tax
articles.title_zh: US warns EU leaders against Big Tech tax
articles.content_orig:
Tech giants could face penalties of up to 5% of their global revenue if found in violation of new online safety rules in Australia.
The country’s Parliament passed the Digital Duty of Care bill Wednesday, Communications Minister Anika Wells said , after the center-left Labor Party government of Prime Minister Anthony Albanese reached a deal with the left-wing Greens party.
Australia has been a world pioneer in legislating protections against harms online. Last December, it implemented a global-first social media ban for residents under 16 , which has had mixed results but has also inspired other countries to follow suit.
To Albanese, the Digital Duty of Care law is the next step. “It’s about Australia ‌taking ⁠action on the side of parents and children, not foreign-owned tech companies,” he told Parliament on Tuesday .
Tech firms like Meta and Apple, many of which are headquartered in the U.S., have said that they want to improve child protection and curb harm on their platforms, though they have pushed back against how broad they say Australia’s laws are. Critics of the Digital Duty of Care law particularly question who gets to decide what counts as harmful content.
David Brat, the U.S. Ambassador to Australia, said he had conveyed the Trump Administration’s objections to the law amendments to Wells on Tuesday.
“Vaguely defined ‘harms,’ backed by penalties of up to 5% of global revenue, will push platforms to censor lawful speech,” Brat posted on social media . “As Australia’s largest foreign investor, the U.S. is concerned with regulations that impose disproportionate compliance burdens on American companies relative to competitors.”
Last month, Wells told the National Press Club that the new law would apply to U.S. President Donald Trump’s Truth Social platform. On Tuesday, she said her ministry was ironing out differences with their American counterparts.
The law amends a collection of internet-related legislation, including Australia’s 2021 Online Safety Act, which set 17 online safety codes and standards to combat unlawful and age-restricted material. Amendments have been pursued for years amid criticisms that previous safeguards were inadequate. Wells said in October that those prior codes “were drafted by big tech for big tech.”
The Digital Duty of Care law, which was introduced in Parliament in October , repeals those prior codes in favor of a broader “ duty of care ” requirement for tech firms, following a 12-month transition period. The duty mimics how Australia regulates other sectors, including aged care and child supervision , commercial vessel and rail safety , and workplace safety , in which businesses and providers are expected to manage risks to health and safety “as much as is reasonably practicable.”
Under the Digital Duty of Care law, platforms must provide risk assessments to regulators at least once a year, and they must notify regulators before they introduce significant changes to their platforms that could allow for new risks of harm, such as “addictive” design features.
The amendments also make it easier for Australian citizens to hold tech companies to account. Previously, one needed to rely on complex legal avenues concerning company negligence and consumer protection. The new law grants Australians the “private right of action,” which means they can directly sue digital platforms for breaching their duty of care.
The new law also implements stronger privacy protections for users, expanded regulatory powers to remove “nudifying” services , and a clarified definition of “hostile attitudes to women”—which now refers to material depicting hatred or the inferiority of women or promoting violence, abuse, exclusion, or the denial of women’s rights.The bill would also require tech firms to allow users in Australia to opt out of a platform’s algorithm and instead choose to see only content from accounts they follow.
It also introduces steeper fines for violations, which Wells said the Australian public demanded. Initially, the proposed maximum penalty was 109 million Australian dollars ($72 million), but it was raised to up to 5% of the violator’s global revenue. The steep fines mirror those in other jurisdictions, including Canada’s proposed 3% penalty in a bill that would require Big Tech to reduce the risk of harmful content and the European Union’s draft 6% fine against companies that push for unfair trade practices.
The Tech Council of Australia, an industry body whose membership includes companies like Google, Microsoft, and LinkedIn, told the Guardian in a statement that it supported the legislation but was concerned over its impact on businesses, particularly in its empowering of individuals to sue.
“A private right of action is a complex undertaking with significant consequences,” a spokesperson said. “How this is implemented is critical, and we need proper consultation to ensure that businesses are not hindered from investing in Australia. If we get this wrong, it will be counterproductive to encouraging innovation in Australia.”
The conservative opposition coalition has called the law “a blank cheque for political censorship.” Senator Sarah Henderson said on Tuesday that the bill compromised current legislation, gave “extensive” powers to the government, and would hurt smaller tech businesses.
“The fact is the digital duty of care should never have seen the light of day,” Henderson said . “This is policy on the run, driven by an insidious agenda to shut down lawful speech and control political debate.”
Wells rejected this. “This is not about what you say online,” she said Wednesday . “It’s about what the platforms do or fail to do online.”

articles.title_orig: At $800 off and a free 5-year warranty: Is this TV the best deal of Black Friday?
articles.title_zh: At $800 off and a free 5-year warranty: Is this TV the best deal of Black Friday?
articles.content_orig:
If you buy something through a link in this article, we may earn commission.
I bought my first 4K TV almost 15 years ago. It wasn't much to write home about: At 43 inches, it was big for me at the time but tiny by modern standards. The "smart" features were a limited handful of streaming apps like Netflix and Amazon, which was still named Prime Instant Video , and most of the 4K content I watched on it came from YouTube. The price for that TV? I don't recall the exact amount, but I know it was four figures and cost me more than a month's rent.
Since then, TVs have gotten better in every way possible — better screen technology, thousands of apps that allow you to choose from millions of hours of 4K movies, TV shows and sporting events, all for a fraction of what I paid for my 43-inch TV. Especially now that Black Friday is in full swing.
If you've been on the fence about upgrading your TV, Costco just made that decision easier to make, with up to $800 off Hisense TVs , including a reasonable 65-inch model for $529 , all the way up to a 100-inch behemoth that will have you believing you are standing on the field at the football game you're watching. And in addition to saving, you get a five-year warranty thrown in at no extra cost.
The sweet spot for most people will probably be the 75-inch, which is down to $699 . If your living room is a little more modest, the 65-inch screen is on sale for $529 .
Going the other direction, the 85-inch is down to $999 for anyone with the square footage to justify it, and the 100-inch (yes, that's a real television size you can actually buy) is $800 off at $999 as well (the 100-inch screen is an LED QLED vs the 85-inch screen's more advanced mini-LED, which is why it's the same price for a larger size).
Before you dismiss an 85-inch or even the 100-inch screen, let me tell you this: I talk and write about TVs a lot, and I have never heard anyone complain about owning too big a TV, that is, once they get it in their house. Just measure to make sure it'll fit before you hit "add to cart."
I am one of those people who easily gets analysis paralysis (though mine generally comes when choosing a workout plan or buying a car, not purchasing a TV). Here's a quick breakdown of what each screen type means:
LED: The screen found on most entry-level TVs. They're affordable, but the least bright and least dynamic picture of the bunch.
OLED: The gold standard for picture quality — perfect blacks, incredible contrast. They're also the most expensive and have a small risk of burn-in over time.
Mini-LED: This is the sweet spot. Brighter than OLED, better contrast than standard LED and usually easier on your wallet than OLED. Great for watching sports, movies and daytime viewing.
QLED: QLED is the same setup as an LED or mini-LED, but with an added layer (called a quantum dot layer) for brighter, punchier colors. A TV can be both LED and QLED or mini-LED and QLED, which is exactly what the QD7 Series is.
ULED: This is Hisense's umbrella term for a TV, like the U65 Pro Series lineup, that features local dimming, wide color gamut, 4K resolution and smooth motion processing.
If your current TV is a standard LED and you've been waiting to upgrade, that moment has arrived, especially if you're eyeing the 100-inch model, which is the best discount of the bunch at $800 off. The increase in picture quality alone from an LED is enough to make the upgrade worth it. That said, if your TV is a recent OLED, the case is harder to make, unless you're looking to go quite a bit bigger.
In addition to the screen technology, all four TVs have a native refresh rate of 144Hz (for reference, most entry-level TVs top out at 60Hz), which means sports look smoother, fast motion stays sharp and, if you're a gamer, the difference will be immediately noticeable.

articles.title_orig: Trump's new tariffs would put rates right back where they were before the Supreme Court stepped in
articles.title_zh: Trump's new tariffs would put rates right back where they were before the Supreme Court stepped in
articles.content_orig:
Oops, something went wrong
A new wave of tariffs from the White House would move overall rates almost exactly back to where they stood in early 2026, according to one initial analysis of the new duties.
The Yale Budget Lab says the newly unveiled plans , if enacted, would return the US to rates seen just before the Supreme Court struck down President Trump's blanket tariffs in February.
Read more: 5 ways to tariff-proof your finances
The estimated overall average statutory rate would rise from the current 11.4% to 13.9% early next year. The rate in February, just before the high court struck down Trump's tariffs enacted under the International Emergency Economic Powers Act of 1977 (IEEPA), was 13.8%.
That remains well below the overall rates seen in 2025. The group estimates that 2025 rates exceeded 15%, peaking at nearly 23% in the weeks after "Liberation Day" in April 2025.
"The administration said it wanted to rebuild the IEEPA tariff regime using Section 301; with this proposal, it will have done so in the aggregate," the group said in its analysis.
The mix of countries bearing the duties will shift slightly, the budget lab noted, with apparel, electronics, and appliances among the biggest categories affected by the new duties.
The reaction from other corners, meanwhile, was that a combination of widespread exemptions, smaller rate changes on other trading partners, and many tariffs that will not be stacked meant the impact could be smaller.
"The latest US tariff announcement is not as alarming as it looks," Stephen Brown, chief North America economist at Capital Economics, wrote in an analysis.
"The increase in the effective tariff rate looks set to be a touch lower than we've been assuming for our forecasts, although the new tariffs will still provide a marginal boost to prices and keep core goods inflation firm into next year," he added, noting that an exact projection from his group will come later on.
US Trade Representative Jamieson Greer downplayed the macroeconomic effects in a CNBC appearance Wednesday, describing the total changes as moves that "really will just top up a few percentage points."
He added that the higher rates on China — the one place where the new tariffs are set to stack on top of other tariffs — are an exception and that the situation for most countries will be less dramatic.
One major trading partner dodged new tariffs this week when it was announced that an investigation in Mexico was still being reviewed. Greer added that recent talks have been going well.
Canada was also not subject to this eight-month investigation, which wrapped up this week and covered China, the European Union, and 14 other nations.
China is set for a 20% baseline "deal rate," which could jump to 40% if ongoing talks break down, while other partners will see much more modest changes.
Rates on some EU goods will jump from 10% to 15% if the new tariffs on excess structural capacity go forward and replace previous tariffs imposed around the issue of forced labor.
Yet the exemption for an array of goods that the EU and others enjoy includes key products such as semiconductors, as well as automobiles, steel, and aluminum, which are subject to a separate tariff authority.
Other goods the Trump administration has carved out in recent months, notably certain energy and food products, will also be exempted.
Ben Werschkul is a Washington correspondent for Yahoo Finance.

articles.title_orig: Germany: 2 suspected Islamists arrested in Heidelberg and Cologne, suspected of plotting synagogue attack
articles.title_zh: Germany: 2 suspected Islamists arrested in Heidelberg and Cologne, suspected of plotting synagogue attack
articles.content_orig:
German prosecutors said on Thursday they had arrested two Iraqi nationals suspected of belonging to a terrorist organization that plotted attacks on Jewish and other targets in Europe, including a Cologne synagogue.
Germany has suffered a series of attacks and plots in recent years, including a fatal attack in July in which a man who pledged allegiance to the Islamic State attacked a Pride celebration in Berlin.
Jewish institutions are under heightened protection after warnings of threats linked to Middle East tensions.
Prosecutors said officers had detained Mostafa Al-R. in Heidelberg and Ameer J. in Cologne , with their full names withheld in line with privacy rules, following 17 raids in the states of Baden-Wuerttemberg, Hesse and North Rhine-Westphalia.
They said Mostafa Al-R. had ties to Mohammad Al-Saadi, an alleged member of an Islamist group that has said it was behind a series of attacks on US, Israeli and Jewish facilities in Europe since March.
Prosecutors said that Al-Saadi, Mostafa Al-R. and others had formed a separate organization in late 2025 to prepare further attacks in Germany and elsewhere in Europe. Prosecutors said Ameer J. was a member of that group.
It recruited external operatives and raised funds for explosive attacks, prosecutors said.
They said that on two consecutive nights in late March, unidentified individuals suspected of acting on the group's behalf and carrying explosive devices had traveled to a synagogue in Cologne and another unspecified location in Europe, but no attacks were carried out for reasons that were unclear.
The two suspects were due to appear before a judge on Thursday, who will decide whether they remain in pre-trial detention.
Authorities said the investigation was launched because of intelligence supplied by Germany's domestic intelligence agency.

The holiday announcement arrives with update 7.15, which also addresses problems with Corvette technology, Colossus cargo and the Analysis Visor on Nintendo Switch.
A scene from No Man’s Sky. The image does not show an FSR comparison. Image: Hello Games / Steam
One fix addresses a problem that could shuffle or lose Corvette technology when travelling to another galaxy. Other fixes cover cargo disappearing from the Colossus flatbed after loading a save and graphical corruption in the Analysis Visor on Nintendo Switch.
The 7.15 notes also list “AMD FSR Upscaling on PC”. However, Hello Games had already documented PC support for FSR 2 in its Waypoint update . The new notes do not identify a version or explain what has changed, so they do not establish that FSR is an entirely new feature for the game.
FSR is an upscaling technology that can render a game at a lower resolution before scaling the image to the display resolution. How useful it is depends on the hardware and settings you choose, so I would check the options on your own PC rather than assume a particular frame-rate gain.
Hello Games is bringing back four community expeditions on a rotating schedule. Image: Hello Games / Steam
Aquarius is the fishing-themed event, with a deep-sea diving suit among its rewards. Remnant follows from December 9 to December 23 and focuses on industrial salvage, including a Gravitino Coil and an heirloom customisation set.
Our Journey Continues runs from December 23 to January 6, celebrating ten years of the game with rewards including a diplodocus companion. The Swarm follows from January 6 to January 20, with armour, equipment and a bonus base part for the most successful team.
These are returning, remixed events rather than four entirely new expeditions. Each has its own window, so check the dates before starting if there is a reward you especially want.
Update 7.15 also includes fixes for vehicles, items and several platforms. Image: Hello Games / Steam
The studio says it is “planning the 2027 roadmap” and has begun work on more content and features. It also says much of the team is working on the upcoming fantasy game Light No Fire , which staff play together on Fridays.
If you are new to the game, Amazon lists No Man’s Sky for PlayStation 5 . That is the PS5 edition; the 7.15 FSR patch note refers specifically to PC, and you do not need to buy another copy to receive the update on a platform where you already own it.

articles.title_orig: Trump Tried to Cripple Huawei. Now It Is Central to China’s A.I. Push.
articles.title_zh: Trump Tried to Cripple Huawei. Now It Is Central to China’s A.I. Push.
articles.content_orig:
China’s biggest technology firm and the world’s largest telecommunications equipment maker has been convicted in the U.S. of stealing trade secrets and defrauding banks about its business in Iran.
Huawei was found guilty on 10 of 12 counts by a jury in Brooklyn on Tuesday. The verdict all but brings to a close an almost eight-year-long criminal case against Huawei and three of its subsidiaries. The sprawling legal case spanned a 12-week trial, dozens of witnesses, and hundreds of motions and filings.
It’s a rare case of U.S. prosecutors securing a conviction against a foreign corporation and could have significant consequences for both Huawei and U.S.-China relations.
The Justice Department first announced charges against Huawei in January 2019 as part of the first-term Trump Administration’s “China Initiative,” a controversial program to investigate and prosecute Chinese influence and espionage in the U.S.
The Shenzhen-based tech giant was found guilty of bank and wire fraud, conspiracy to steal trade secrets, and violations of U.S. sanctions. It faces massive potential penalties, including fines, forfeiture, and restitution. Sentencing is set for September 2027, with motions in advance of sentencing expected to start in the third week of January.
“Few crimes are as serious as Huawei’s decades-long pattern of endangering U.S. national security, violating the sanctity of U.S. commerce, and impeding the enforcement of U.S. laws,” U.S. Attorney Joseph Nocella Jr. said .
James Barnacle Jr., assistant director in charge of the FBI’s New York office, added, “Huawei’s success was built on deception and theft, and the FBI will never hesitate to pursue those who profit by breaking the law.”
The jury, however, acquitted Huawei of the most serious charge: racketeering conspiracy under the Racketeer Influenced and Corrupt Organisations Act (RICO).
Huawei’s attorney Brian Heberlig argued that U.S. prosecutors “began with guilt and worked backwards,” basing their claims of conspiracy on isolated incidents.
Huawei’s success, he said, is “about competition, not conspiracy. Innovation, not theft. Ordinary business dealings, not criminal conduct.”
Heberlig told reporters that the company will appeal the case.
“We believe the government’s remaining charges are equally without legal or factual merit,” Huawei said in a statement . “We will thoroughly review the relevant verdicts and take all necessary legal actions to defend our rights and interests.”
Huawei lawyer Brian Heberlig speaks to reporters outside federal court in Brooklyn, N.Y., on Nov. 24, 2026. Larry Neumeister—AP
Huawei was convicted of conspiracy to steal trade secrets from U.S. companies over two decades. Its alleged theft includes router source code from Cisco Systems, semiconductor equipment from CNEX Labs, robotic phone testing equipment from T-Mobile, antenna technology from Quintel, and networking equipment information from Fujitsu Network Communications. The jury also found Huawei and its subsidiaries guilty of violating the International Emergency Economic Powers Act and money laundering.
During the trial, which began Sept. 8, the jury watched a video that prosecutors said showed a Huawei engineer unbolting and detaching the arm of a high-speed T-Mobile testing robot and slipping it into his backpack. The engineer said he found the piece in his bag, calling the incident a “mistake,” and returned it the next day after T-Mobile reported it missing, but not before a visiting engineer from China allegedly measured and photographed the robotic arm, according to prosecutors. Huawei later fired the employee.
Prosecutors also argued that Huawei had hired a professor to gain access to a circuit board developed by CNEX.
“Huawei cultivated a culture of crime and corruption, and that crime was an important business strategy,” U.S. prosecutor Taylor Stout said in his opening statement.
Huawei’s attorneys called 15 witnesses to give evidence that the company’s success came from its own innovation. The attorneys cited the company’s 110,000-person research and development team and its over 165,000 patents. Heberlig said prosecutors had “cherry-picked” instances of employee misconduct that were not representative of Huawei’s company culture.
Prosecutors also argued that Huawei deliberately deceived global banks, including HSBC, BNP Paribas, and Standard Chartered, about its business in Iran and North Korea, which are both subject to U.S. sanctions. Huawei allegedly presented its Iran subsidiary, Skycom Tech, as an independent entity to skirt sanctions.
The jury, however, rejected the government’s assertion that Huawei had conspired in a racketeering scheme to expand its global business. If the company had been convicted of the RICO charge, it could have faced potential forfeiture of parts of its enterprise.
“It’s hard not to have profoundly mixed emotions from the verdict we just heard,” Heberlig, Huawei’s attorney, told reporters. The RICO charge, he said, “alleged that the company was corrupt from top to bottom, that it had a corporate culture and policy of cheating, stealing, and lying, and the jury found the company not guilty on that charge.”
The jury also acquitted the company of conspiring to obstruct a federal grand jury investigation.
The legal case is among the most extensive against a corporation, involving millions of documents in evidence, covering source code, financial records, and emails. Jurors spent five days, beginning Nov. 18, deliberating the case.
“Rarely has a jury had to commit so much of their personal time to a trial,” U.S. District Judge Ann Donnelly, who oversaw the case, said.
The case also took a winding path before the trial even began. It was delayed for years during the COVID-19 pandemic. In 2022, U.S. prosecutors also charged two Chinese intelligence officers with trying to bribe a U.S. government employee with $61,000 in bitcoin to steal evidence and information about the case.
The case could have ramifications on the U.S.’s relationship with China. The verdict comes days after President Donald Trump met with Chinese President Xi Jinping in Shenzhen. It also comes amid tensions over Nvidia CEO Jensen Huang’s affair with an alleged Chinese spy , which has renewed calls by U.S. lawmakers for tighter restrictions on A.I. chip sales to China .
Huawei, which is privately held, is one of China’s largest and most famous companies. The company reported 880.9 billion RMB ($126 billion) in revenue last year. It employs more than 200,000 employees globally and operates in more than 170 countries.
The case spawned a diplomatic crisis in 2018, when Canadian authorities detained Huawei Chief Financial Officer Meng Wanzhou, who is also the daughter of the company’s founder, at the U.S.’s request. Meng had been secretly indicted on U.S. charges of bank and wire fraud.
Meng pleaded not guilty to criminal charges and fought extradition to the U.S. while under house arrest in Vancouver for nearly three years. She entered a deferred prosecution agreement in 2021, which acknowledged that she had misled an HSBC banker about Huawei’s relationship with Skycom, after which she returned to China. A federal judge dismissed the charges against her with prejudice in December 2022. The HSBC executive Meng had met with in 2013 testified in the Brooklyn trial.
The first charges were announced as Washington and Beijing were locked in a trade war.
Since the first-term Trump Administration launched the “China Initiative” in 2018, federal prosecutors have secured convictions against a number of foreign nationals, but corporate cases have had mixed outcomes. Taiwan’s United Microelectronics pleaded guilty to stealing trade secrets in 2020, and China’s Hytera Communications pleaded guilty to conspiring to steal trade secrets in 2025. Chinese chipmaker Fujian Jinhua was acquitted in 2024. A separate federal case in Seattle against two Huawei subsidiaries has been repeatedly delayed, with a trial date set for October

articles.title_orig: China firmly opposes proposed US Section 301 tariffs
articles.title_zh: China firmly opposes proposed US Section 301 tariffs
articles.content_orig:
China on Thursday said it firmly opposes proposed US Section 301 tariffs on imports from 14 economies, including China, and urged Washington to correct its course and resolve the issue through dialogue and consultation.
Speaking at a news conference in Beijing, Ministry of Commerce spokesman He Yadong said China would closely follow developments and reserve the right to take necessary measures to safeguard its legitimate rights and interests.
He described the US investigations as “a typical act of unilateralism”, saying they seriously undermine the international economic order and violate World Trade Organization rules.
ALSO READ: China's high-tech FDI surges 31.3% in first 10 months
The Office of the US Trade Representative on Nov 25 released the findings of its investigations into alleged manufacturing overcapacity and proposed additional tariffs under Section 301 of the Trade Act of 1974.
“Some countries are pursuing protectionism in the name of addressing overcapacity, politicizing normal market competition and turning industrial development issues into political tools,” He said.
He said such measures would leave those countries’ structural problems unresolved, destabilize global industrial and supply chains, disrupt industrial cooperation and push up global inflation.
They would also harm businesses and consumers and pose long-term, systemic risks to global economic growth, he added.
On July 28, the Ministry of Commerce released a position paper on so-called overcapacity, calling for a comprehensive and objective assessment of global industrial capacity and for greater international cooperation.

articles.title_orig: U.S. chip curbs and distillation crackdown to impact Chinese AI model progress
articles.title_zh: U.S. chip curbs and distillation crackdown to impact Chinese AI model progress
articles.content_orig:
Nvidia chip sellers are seeking new buyers for the semiconductor giant's hardware, three people told CNBC, after the Trump administration tightened rules to curb Chinese companies' remote access to the most advanced artificial-intelligence systems.
Companies have put an unusually high volume of Nvidia graphics processing units, or GPUs, on the market since new measures restricting Chinese companies renting access to advanced Nvidia chips were announced on Nov. 16, the people said.
Jack Duhamel, president of AI infrastructure marketplace GPU Mart, and two people familiar with the matter told CNBC the surge in GPUs for sale was directly attributable to the new rule. Duhamel added that one company looking to sell Nvidia chips told GPU Mart the sale was related to the new rule.
The two people said it appeared chip sellers were seeking to offload them because they were originally for use in data centers in which Chinese companies would rent access. They asked not to be named because they were discussing private information.
The Department of Commerce's Bureau of Industry and Security, or BIS, announced an interim final rule as part of a clampdown on Chinese companies bypassing export controls, which effectively ban the sale of the most advanced Nvidia chips to China, by accessing them remotely in overseas data centers. The rule came into effect on Nov. 19.
Deals to find buyers for thousands of B300 GPUs, one of Nvidia's most advanced offerings, have been floated since the rule was announced, said Duhamel and one of the people.
Nvidia declined to comment. BIS did not immediately respond to a request for comment.
Nvidia has been facing increasing scrutiny from U.S. lawmakers over Chinese companies' access to its advanced chips.
The chip giant warned its customers that the proposed Remote Access Security Act — which has passed the House of Representatives but is yet to pass the Senate — would give the U.S. government broader authority to control access to cloud services, potentially exposing both parties to "legal action," sources previously told CNBC.
In July, the U.S. accused a Chinese AI lab, Moonshot AI , of accessing Nvidia chips via a facility in Thailand. CNBC reported on Nov. 5 that the company had sought access to the chips via data centers in Europe.
U.S. Trade Representative Jamieson Greer told CNBC's "Squawk Box" on Wednesday that the new rule announced last week was intended to close "loopholes."
"For a long time, we have not allowed the sale of Blackwell chips, which are the highest AI chips or similar chips to China directly," he said.
"Some rules were issued by the Commerce Department last week to close off indirect access, either smuggling through places like Southeast Asia or remote access from data centers in third countries."
During Nvidia's third-quarter earnings call on Nov. 17, then-interim CEO Colette Kress said the company was still studying the controls, but expected performance to remain strong because demand for chips far exceeded supply.

articles.content_orig:
Fast-fashion retailer Shein has agreed to pay $100 million to settle Federal Trade Commission allegations that it misled customers.
The FTC says the money will be used to compensate customers harmed by the company's practices.
The agency said tens of thousands of customers reported receiving their orders late, while others never received them at all. Shein allegedly failed to notify customers of shipping delays as required by law.
RELATED STORY | Fashion giant Shein facing new scrutiny from US regulators
The FTC also accused Shein of publishing positive product reviews while suppressing or deleting negative ones.
Investigators also found that some cotton Shein advertised as U.S.-grown originated in China.
Under the proposed settlement, Shein would be required to stop misrepresenting delivery times, suppressing negative reviews and making deceptive claims about its supply chain. The company would also have to provide adequate customer service.

articles.title_orig: U.S. tariff-hike threats pile pressure on partners to sign trade deals
articles.title_zh: U.S. tariff-hike threats pile pressure on partners to sign trade deals
articles.content_orig:
The Trump administration has unveiled a fresh tariff salvo on more than a dozen trading partners, with China, Vietnam, and India facing some of the steepest potential rates and mounting pressure to conclude trade deals with Washington.
The proposed tariffs, framed as curbing excess industrial capacity, start at 15% for the European Union, South Korea, Switzerland and Taiwan and rise to as much as 35% for Vietnam.
The U.S. Trade Representative's Office said it intends to cap the new duties at lower levels for countries that have completed trade deals or are still negotiating with Washington.
The overall impact on the region is likely to be limited, said Mark Williams, chief Asia economist at Capital Economics. The proposal "puts most of the targeted countries back where they were earlier in the year," he said, after the Supreme Court struck down Trump's emergency tariffs in February.
Still, the proposal could give some countries an incentive to speed up trade talks in order to lock in lower tariff rates, analysts said.
On Wednesday, U.S. Trade Representative Jamieson Greer said that the new policy likely will not take effect for months, with a senior U.S. official saying the duties could take effect as early as January.
China faces a capped rate of 20%, on top of an existing 25% tariff imposed during President Donald Trump's first term. The rate could rise to 40% if the trade truce reached in South Korea last October is not extended beyond January, the USTR said.
Beijing has rejected Washington's claim of excess capacity while vowing to take measures necessary to protect its rights.
On Thursday, Chinese Commerce Ministry spokesperson He Yadong called on Washington to "rectify its wrongdoing and return to the right track of resolving issues through dialogue."
He was responding to Washington's plan to raise tariffs following its Section 301 investigations, while the ministry also urged the U.S. to implement $30 billion of reciprocal tariff cuts agreed by the two sides in late September.
The renewed tensions come despite several conciliatory meetings between Trump and Chinese President Xi Jinping this year, as well as what Williams described as Trump's "apparent lack of concern" about allegations that Chinese technology firms have circumvented U.S. chip export controls.
The two leaders are expected to meet for a fourth time this year at the Group of 20 leaders summit in Miami in December.
"While not happy, Beijing seems prepared to live with the new rates provided that they don't exceed 20%," said Wendy Cutler, senior vice president at the Asia Society Policy Institute.
By retaining the option to raise levies if bilateral talks deteriorate, Washington is using the tariffs as leverage to "secure expected shipments of critical minerals and rare earths, and further purchases of U.S. agricultural goods," Cutler said.
Washington has warned that tariffs on Chinese goods could double to 40% if the USTR finds that Beijing is not engaging. "If the trade war did start up again, today's measures provide the U.S. with some ammunition," Williams said.
Even the sweeping actions against the other 13 trading partners appear aimed squarely at China, said Williams, who tallied that the word "China" appears 253 times in the USTR's report on Vietnam, and 315 times in the document on the European Union.
"Foremost among the 'unreasonable acts, policies, and practices' that these countries are criticised for is being slow to restrict imports and FDI from China," Williams said.
While the proposed tariffs generally lift average rates only modestly, India and Vietnam stand out because of the wider gaps between the rates they would face with and without a deal, analysts said.
India and Vietnam face proposed tariffs of 25% and 35%, respectively, but those rates could fall sharply to 17% and 20% if ongoing talks with the U.S. produce reciprocal trade agreements.
The two countries have "a strong incentive" to conclude deals with Washington to secure the lower rates, Cutler said.
Vietnam's trade ministry said Thursday that it was working with the U.S. to complete a trade deal as soon as possible, according to Reuters . India could also gain an edge over some Asian rivals through comparatively lower levies if New Delhi concludes its long-pending trade deal with Washington.
Singapore faces a similar challenge. The proposal sets a maximum potential rate of 20% on its exports, net of existing Section 301 tariffs, which could fall to 10% if it reaches an agreement on reciprocal trade with the U.S. or concludes other negotiations addressing the USTR's findings, according to Singapore's Ministry of Energy, Trade and Industry .
The ministry said it disagreed with the findings and was "very disappointed" with the proposed action, arguing that it failed to account for the structure of Singapore's economy.
Under the U.S.-Singapore Free Trade Agreement, Singapore imposes zero tariffs on U.S. goods, while the U.S. has run a trade surplus with the city-state for more than 20 years, the ministry said. That surplus grew to $33 billion in 2025 from $27 billion in 2024.
Singapore said it would submit further comments during the public consultation period and urge the USTR to reconsider.
Exemptions for semiconductors and other electronics should cushion the impact on South Korea and Taiwan, whose economies are heavily concentrated in those sectors, analysts said.
The USTR singled out South Korea for its concentration in memory-chip production and what it described as outsized government support. Yet it excluded the country's chips from the proposed excess-capacity tariffs.
Taiwan, which faces an excess-capacity tariff cap of 15%, also benefits from exemptions for other electronics, including mobile phones and networking equipment. Its effective tariff rate would rise to about 9% from 6%, Williams estimated.
— CNBC's Evelyn Cheng contributed to this report.
